# Psalm 62 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview / Title

**“For the choirmaster. According to Jeduthun. A Psalm of David.”** Jeduthun was one of David's appointed musicians for public worship (1 Chronicles 16:41; 25:1–3). Spurgeon notes that “the sons of Jeduthun were porters or doorkeepers” (1 Chronicles 16:42) — those who serve well make the best singers. The psalm is also paired with Jeduthun in the title of Psalms 39 and 77.

https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-62/

Psalm 62 is unusual among David's psalms: it comes from a time of trouble, yet **contains no petition, no fear, and no prayer**. It is pure faith and confidence. The Hebrew particle *ak* (“only”/“alone”/“truly”) appears six times (vv. 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 9), giving the psalm an insistent, earnest tone of exclusive trust.

https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps062.php

---

## v. 1 — “In God alone my soul finds rest; my salvation comes from Him.”

**Traditional reading:** The Hebrew literally reads, “unto God (is) silence my soul.” David describes a surrendered, quiet waiting — not a silence of prayerlessness, but of a soul that has ceased murmuring and rests in submission. Gill explains it as “not as to prayer, but as to murmuring; patiently and quietly waiting for salvation until the Lord's time.” The LXX and Vulgate render it “shall be in subjection to,” emphasising resignation to God's will. Spurgeon adds that “the presence of God alone could awe his heart into quietude, submission, rest, and acquiescence.”

https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/62.htm
https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps062.php
https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/62.htm

The word “truly” (or “only”) sets the tone: faith that rests only partly on the Lord is vain confidence. “To wait on God alone is spiritual chastity” (Spurgeon).

https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps062.php

Derek Kidner comments, “The words have all been said – or perhaps no words will come – and the issue rests with Him alone.”

https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-62/

David Guzik (Enduring Word) notes that David begins not by describing his crisis but by declaring his confidence in God — a rare approach among his psalms.

https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-62/

**Reformed/Baptist distinctive:** Spurgeon preached that “God only is our salvation” is the essence of Calvinism: “If anyone should ask you what you mean by a Calvinist, you may reply, ‘He is one who says, salvation is of the Lord.’” He adds, “Tell me anything that departs from this and it will be a heresy.”

https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/god-alone-the-salvation-of-his-people

---

## v. 2 — “He alone is my rock and my salvation. He is my fortress; I will never be shaken.”

**Traditional reading:** David piles up images of security: rock, salvation, fortress (or “high tower”). Spurgeon notes the metaphor of a rock would awaken grateful memories — David had often hidden in rocky caverns. The “fortress” is a bolder image: the believer dwells in God as a warrior in a defiant tower.

https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps062.php

**“I will never be shaken”** (or “I shall not be greatly moved” in some translations): David acknowledges his personal weakness might cause *some* disturbance, but faith prevents any *great* disturbance. Spurgeon: “Moved, as one says, ‘but not removed.’ Moved like a ship at anchor which swings with the tide, but is not swept away by the tempest.”

https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps062.php

Ellicott notes that “defence” properly means “high tower” — an important metaphor because it contrasts with the “tottering wall” of v. 3.

https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/62.htm

---

## v. 3 — “How long will you threaten a man? Will all of you throw him down like a leaning wall or a tottering fence?”

**Traditional reading:** David confronts his enemies, marveling at their dogged persistence in malice. There is debate about whether the “leaning wall and tottering fence” describes David (viewed by enemies as ready to collapse) or his enemies (who will themselves be destroyed). The NKJV presents the enemies as the leaning wall; the ESV presents David as the one being battered. Spurgeon held the first sense: “Boastful persecutors bulge and swell with pride, but they are only as a bulging wall ready to fall in a heap.”

https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps062.php
https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-62/

Gill notes that the warning “ye shall be slain all of you” is an aggravation of their folly — their mischief would recoil on themselves. Some Jewish interpreters read it as a prayer (“may ye be slain”).

https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/62.htm

---

## v. 4 — “They fully intend to cast him down from his lofty perch; they delight in lies; with their mouths they bless, but inwardly they curse. Selah”

**Traditional reading:** The enemies’ single-minded purpose (“they only consult”) is to bring down the man of God from his position of honour. Gill suggests this may refer to Absalom and Ahithophel's conspiracy to pull David from the throne. The enemies are two-faced — outwardly blessing but inwardly cursing. Spurgeon notes: “Flattery has ever been a favourite weapon with the enemies of good men.” *Selah* calls for a pause to “consider with astonishment the futile rancour of unholy men, and the perfect security of such as rest themselves upon the Lord.”

https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps062.php
https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/62.htm

The word “only” (*ak*) appears here too — their sole consultation is to cast him down, just as David's sole trust is in God.

https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-62/

---

## v. 5 — “Rest in God alone, O my soul, for my hope comes from Him.”

**Traditional reading:** David shifts from *stating* his confidence (v. 1) to *commanding* his soul to maintain it. Kidner: “David now urges on himself the silence which he simply stated in verse 1.” Gill suggests “perhaps some new temptation might arise, and David's soul began to be uneasy and impatient; for frames are very changeable things; and therefore he encourages it to be still and quiet.”

https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-62/
https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/62.htm

Trapp (cited in Guzik): “They trust not God at all who trust him not alone. He that stands with one foot on a rock, and another foot upon a quicksand, will sink and perish.”

https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-62/

The Pulpit Commentary homiletics notes this silence as (1) a sign of faith, (2) a record of inner conflict already fought, (3) the soul's complete acquiescence, and (4) a foreshadowing of victory.

https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/psalms/62.htm

**Reformed/Baptist:** John Piper (Desiring God) writes that desperation is one of the most effective instructors in trusting God. David “preaches to his troubled, weak, vulnerable, fragile soul.” He notes that “to be brought to a place where God is our only real hope is a merciful experience.”

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/waiting-for-god-alone

---

## v. 6 — “He alone is my rock and my salvation; He is my fortress; I will not be shaken.”

**Traditional reading:** David repeats v. 2 almost verbatim, but with a crucial difference: in v. 2 he said “I shall not be *greatly* moved”; here he says “I shall not be moved” at all. Maclaren: “There may be deep meaning in the slight omission of ‘greatly’ in the second refrain. Confidence has grown.” Gill: “his faith gets fresh strength and rigour.” Faith grows as it is exercised.

https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-62/
https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/62.htm
https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-62-god-only

---

## v. 7 — “My salvation and my honor rest on God, my strong rock; my refuge is in God.”

**Traditional reading:** David now adds “my glory” (or “my honour”) to the catalogue of what rests on God. Gill explains that God is the author of all David's temporal honour and dignity, his spiritual glory (righteousness and grace), and the eternal glory he awaited. Spurgeon highlights the repeated use of “my”: “Observe how the Psalmist brands his own initials upon every name which he rejoicingly gives to his God — my expectation, my rock, my salvation, my glory, my strength, my refuge.”

https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps062.php
https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/62.htm

---

## v. 8 — “Trust in Him at all times, O people; pour out your hearts before Him. God is our refuge. Selah”

**Traditional reading:** David turns from personal confidence to teaching others. He urges trust “at all times” — no moment excepted, in adversity as well as prosperity. The exhortation to “pour out your heart before Him” shows that the God who is a rock is not cold or insensitive. Spurgeon: “Turn the vessel of your soul upside down in his secret presence, and let your inmost thoughts, desires, sorrows, and sins be poured out like water.” Le Blanc (cited by Spurgeon): “Pour it out as water. Not as milk, whose colour remains. Not as wine, whose savour remains. Not as honey, whose taste remains. But as water, of which, when it is poured out, nothing remains.”

https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps062.php
https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-62/

The Pulpit Commentary notes that “pouring out your heart” fits with “waiting silently” — silent submission does not contradict heart-felt prayer; both are appropriate.

https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/psalms/62.htm

Bible.org (Steven Cole) comments: “Sadly, I’ve heard supposedly Christian psychologists say that it is useless, pat advice to tell hurting people to trust in God. I don’t know what Bible they were reading!”

https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-62-god-only

---

## v. 9 — “Lowborn men are but a vapor, the exalted but a lie. Weighed on the scale, they go up; together they are but a vapor.”

**Traditional reading:** David explains *why* we should not trust in man. Whether “sons of Adam” (low degree) or “sons of men” (high degree), all are “lighter than vapour.” Kidner: “The point is not so much that we have nothing to fear from man (as in Psalm 27:1ff.), as that we have nothing to hope from him.” Spurgeon: “Common men can give no help. They are vanity … Rich men are a lie. They promise much, but perform nothing.”

https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps062.php
https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-62/

Gill: if you put men and vanity on a balance scale, vanity weighs heavier — the scale with men “goes up.” The word “lighter” is not in the Hebrew but is rightly supplied.

https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/62.htm

VanGemeren (cited by Guzik) notes that the distinction between low and high may simply be Hebrew poetic parallelism — a general reference to all mankind: “mankind is but a breath; mankind is but a lie.”

https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-62/

---

## v. 10 — “Place no trust in extortion, or false hope in stolen goods. If your riches increase, do not set your heart upon them.”

**Traditional reading:** David warns against three wrong objects of trust: oppression, robbery, and riches — “even honestly gained” ones. Gill: “If riches increase in a lawful way … set not your heart upon them.” Spurgeon: “To bow an immortal spirit to the constant contemplation of fading possessions is extreme folly.” Maclaren: “Whether rightly or wrongly won, they are wrongly used if they are trusted in.”

https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps062.php
https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/62.htm
https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-62/

Kidner notes that 1 Timothy 6:17 may allude to this verse, and that “absorption with riches counts as no less perilous than a life of crime.”

https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-62/

---

## v. 11 — “God has spoken once; I have heard this twice: that power belongs to God”

**Traditional reading:** “Once … twice” is a Hebrew numerical device for emphasis — not literal counting, but meaning God has impressed this truth repeatedly on David's heart. Matthew Henry: “To some God speaks twice and they will not hear once; but to others he speaks but once, and they hear twice.” Gill: “One word of his is more to be confided in … than all the men and things in the world.”

https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps062.php
https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/62.htm
https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-62-god-only

**Jewish mystical interpretation:** Gill notes that “the ancient Cabalists among the Jews have endeavoured, from this passage, to establish a Trinity in unity,” reading “once” and “twice” as three superior *Sephirot*.

https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/62.htm

---

## v. 12 — “and loving devotion to You, O Lord. For You will repay each man according to his deeds.”

**Traditional reading:** David pairs God's power with His *hesed* (lovingkindness, covenant love, mercy). Spurgeon: “This tender attribute sweetens the grand thought of his power: the divine strength will not crush us, but will be used for our good.” Perowne (cited by Boice): “Power without love is brutality, and love without power is weakness. Power is the strong foundation of love, and love is the beauty and the crown of power.”

https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-62/
https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps062.php

**“For You render to each man according to his work”** — this seems to speak of justice, yet David places it under mercy. Spurgeon offers two interpretations: (1) God graciously rewards the poor, imperfect works of His people — a display of mercy; (2) God metes out strength equal to our assigned work. Gill: “Power in punishing the wicked according to their deserts, and mercy in rewarding the saints, not in a way of merit, or of debt, but of grace.” The Pulpit Commentary notes this pairing of power and mercy is “the guarantee of righteous rule.”

https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps062.php
https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/62.htm
https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/psalms/62.htm

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

**Reformed / Calvinist:** Spurgeon explicitly uses v. 2 (“He only is my rock and my salvation”) as the banner of Calvinism — God alone saves, without human cooperation. “I cannot find in Scripture any other doctrine than this. It is the essence of the Bible.”

https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/god-alone-the-salvation-of-his-people

**Baptist:** Spurgeon's two sermons on this psalm (Nos. 80 and 144) emphasise that experimental knowledge of God as our *only* salvation is “the greatest of all experience.” Doctrine must be proved in life. The great duty flowing from this doctrine is to give God *all* trust, *all* love, *all* glory — not to have “two Gods, two Christs, two friends.”

https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/god-alone-the-salvation-of-his-people
https://www.ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons03/sermons03.xxxvii.html

**Evangelical / broadly Reformed (Bible.org / Steven Cole):** Emphasises that vv. 5–7 show David *talking to himself*, preaching truth to his own soul rather than listening to his anxieties. Martyn Lloyd-Jones is cited: “Have you realized that most of your unhappiness in life is due to the fact that you are listening to yourself instead of talking to yourself?”

https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-62-god-only

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Guzik's commentary does not significantly depart from the traditional evangelical reading but emphasises the experiential, personal dimension — the need to “actively command our souls to remain silent.” The tone is pastoral and application-focused.

https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-62/

*(Note: I was unable to search for distinctively Methodist/Wesleyan, Lutheran, or Anglican treatments due to search limits. No distinct denominational differences emerged in the sources searched beyond the Reformed/Baptist emphasis on monergistic salvation.)*
